articles.title: Fall of the centre: on the public discontent in France
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: When Emmanuel Macron came to power in 2017 , at age 39, he promised to keep extremist political forces at bay, build a new France through his ‘revolution’, rejuvenate economic growth, manage debt and create employment opportunities. Nine years later, with six months to go for France’s next presidential election, Mr. Macron, whose approval rating is at an abysmally low 15%, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu , who lacks a parliamentary majority, are struggling to restore order in a country battered by economic woes, street protests, violent riots and a surging far right. Even in France, where protests are part of the political culture, Saturday’s (October 17, 2026) riots and looting were a shock with at least 3,000 businesses and shops damaged. Municipal halls were attacked and buildings set on fire , including the 19 th -century Limoges town hall. Some 2,400 people were arrested and Prime Minister Lecornu called for local curfews . The trigger for the unrest was a move by Mr. Lecornu to pass budget proposals raising some taxes and freezing spending on social programmes. When school students hit the streets with demands for better educational facilities, the government responded with force and tear gas. But its heavy-handed response helped the student protest snowball into an anti-government movement, culminating in riots.

To understand the precarious situation France is in today, all one has to do is to look at the macroeconomic numbers. Growth remains sluggish with the economy estimated to expand by a mere 0.8% in 2026, while the unemployment rate stands at 8.3%. The core problem is the country’s public finances. France’s national debt stands at 120% of GDP, the third highest in the eurozone, after Greece and Italy. The French Treasury’s debt servicing bill is expected to reach about €60 billion in 2026. When Mr. Macron came to power, he reduced corporate taxes and sought to restrain public spending to stimulate growth. But growth remained sluggish while public debt ballooned. When protests gripped the country in 2018-19, he offered economic concessions, but with no long-term solutions to the structural problems the French economy was facing. In 2024, he called snap elections to blunt the far-right momentum. After the elections, he invited a leader from smaller blocs to form a government to keep the left-wing New Popular Front, the largest bloc, out of power, deepening the political crisis and weakening his position. This is Emmanuel Macron’s legacy. Worse, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right, anti-immigrant National Rally, could exploit the chaos and public anger to her benefit ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

articles.title: Unknown vulnerabilities: on the cybersecurity advisory by CERT-In
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The cybersecurity advisory by the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has outlined two threat vectors vis-à-vis Indian commercial and government IT infrastructure: AI companies testing autonomous agents exceeding their designated operational constraints and bad actors weaponising open-source agentic AI tools for automated reconnaissance and exploitation. However, the organisations affected by recent breaches that the advisory was based on did not detect them: they came to light in the AI companies’ disclosures and CERT-In operations. Aside from developers allowing experimental systems to act outside their authorised bounds, the advisory highlights two problems for India — existing arrangements focus on cybersecurity incidents after they are revealed; and the implicated organisations being found under-prepared for the DPDP Act — to be enforced from 2027, including steep penalties on entities not maintaining reasonable safeguards against breaches. While CERT-In observed or received reports of 29.4 lakh incidents in 2025, it does not routinely publish postmortem analyses and is exempt from the RTI Act. As a result, public accountability is also weak: CERT-In found that the AI agents and/or bad actors exploited vulnerabilities, including exposed passwords, that are known security problems separate from AI agents’ abilities.

AI companies and labs have made several disclosures this year of agents unexpectedly breaching real-world infrastructure worldwide during testing. For India, however, the legal boundaries specified by the IT Act 2000 leave open an accountability gap for autonomous agents without the backing of human intentions. A more specific lacuna is that while CERT-In requires an organisation to report an intrusion within six hours, many organisations remain incapable of, or unwilling to, discover it. The reporting deadline itself has not ensured detection. Overall, the national cybersecurity landscape is fragmented across a pastiche of enforceable requirements in some domains, advisory technical standards in others, and narrow AI-specific accountability in yet others. As human and autonomous threat actors become more sophisticated, India needs to leapfrog to a landscape with enforceable risk-based requirements for both testing and defending against autonomous agents; better spotting unauthorised access, especially in the public sector; and a legal safe-harbour for security research conducted in good faith, in line with CERT-In policy. CERT-In should also publish more information, anonymised where necessary, which includes remediation outcomes and whether the affected individuals were informed. Finally, the government should also review the exemption for CERT-In from the RTI Act as such a sweeping exemption is unnecessary for effective cyber-defence.

articles.title: Cyclonic storm likely by October 26; heavy rain in Coastal Andhra from October 27: IMD
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A low-pressure area has formed over the east-central and adjoining south-east Bay of Bengal, and it is expected to intensify into a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay by Monday (October 26, 2026) morning, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said on Friday (October 23, 2026). The system is then forecast to move towards the north Andhra Pradesh and adjoining south Odisha coasts.

In a special message, the IMD’s Cyclone Warning Centre in Visakhapatnam said the low-pressure area formed at around 5.30 a.m. on Friday under the influence of an upper-air cyclonic circulation that was over the south-east and adjoining east-central Bay of Bengal on Thursday.

Under the influence of yesterday's upper-air cyclonic circulation over Southeast and adjoining Eastcentral #Bay_of_Bengal, a low pressure area formed over Eastcentral and adjoining Southeast Bay of Bengal at 0530 hours IST of today, the 23rd October, 2026. It is most likely to persist over the same region and intensify into a depression on 24th October, 2026. Thereafter, it is very likely to move west-northwestwards and intensify further into a deep #depression on 25th October & into a #cyclonic_storm over the Westcentral Bay of Bengal by 26th October morning. It would then continue to intensify further and move west-northwestwards towards North #Andhra_Pradesh and adjoining South #Odisha coasts during subsequent 2 days.

The system is most likely to remain over the same region and intensify into a depression on Saturday (October 24), the IMD said. It is then very likely to move west-northwestwards, intensifying into a deep depression on Sunday (October 25) and a cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by Monday morning. It would continue to intensify and move west-northwestwards towards the north Andhra Pradesh and south Odisha coasts over the following two days, the bulletin said.

Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (APSDMA) Managing Director Prakhar Jain said on Friday that the State was likely to receive widespread rain under the influence of the system. He advised the public and farmers to take precautions in advance, and asked fishermen to return to the coast without delay.

On Thursday, the IMD’s Amaravati centre had said the system may bring heavy to very heavy rain to parts of Coastal Andhra Pradesh from October 27. For October 27 and 28, it issued an ‘alert’ (be prepared) for heavy to very heavy rain at isolated places in Alluri Sitharama Raju (ASR), Kakinada, East Godavari, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema, Eluru, West Godavari and NTR districts, and in Yanam. A ‘watch’ (be updated) for heavy rain at isolated places covers 10 other districts on both days, including Visakhapatnam.

P.L.N. Murthy, Head of the IMD’s Cyclone Warning Centre in Visakhapatnam, said on Thursday that if the system continued to intensify and became a cyclonic system, it might cross the coast between Machilipatnam and Visakhapatnam. He added that in El Niño years, most post-monsoon cyclones in the Bay cross the coast south of 17° N. The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) models, Mr. Murthy said, indicated that very heavy rainfall was likely across northern Andhra Pradesh by October 27.

The IMD’s Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre for tropical cyclones, New Delhi, said on Thursday that models differed on the system’s strength: some, including the ECMWF, pointed to a very severe cyclonic storm, while AI-based models showed a cyclonic storm at most.

Heavy rain lashed Nellore and Prakasam districts on Thursday under the influence of the cyclonic circulation. Low-lying areas in several parts of both districts were waterlogged, and commuters faced traffic jams.

In the 24 hours ending 8.30 a.m. on Thursday, Thottambedu in Tirupati district recorded 40.2 mm and Rapur in Nellore district 40 mm, the highest reported. During the day on Thursday, Nellore recorded 22 mm of rain, Kavali 15 mm and Cuddapah 13 mm, the IMD’s Amaravati centre said.

Kurnool had the highest maximum temperature among the stations listed, 35.3° C, 2.6° C above normal, while Ongole, Narsapur and Nellore were 3.9° C to 4.6° C below normal. Amaravati recorded 33.5° C, up 0.1° C from the previous day, and Visakhapatnam 32.7° C, 0.9° C above normal.
Thunderstorms with lightning and strong winds of 30 to 40 kmph are likely at isolated places over Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema on Saturday.

articles.title: Golden Chariot revamped, fully booked for the first time
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Golden Chariot operating under the Pride of Karnataka itinerary has been revamped for the 2026–27 season. The rooms, food, and beverage options have all been upgraded. For the first time, the trip has been completely booked, with a full house of 75 guests embarking on the first trip on Saturday. Apart from guests from across the country, many guests are also from Spain, a senior Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation (KSTDC) official said.

Minister for Tourism K.J. George (centre), along with Tourism Department and IRCTC officials, inspected the Golden Chariot train at Cantonment Railway Station in Bengaluru on October 23, 2026. The train will start its journey on October 24 from KSR Railway Station at Majestic and head to Mysuru as part of the Pride of Karnataka itinerary. | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

“We have 75 seats and all of them have been booked for the first time. The full booking for the first journey is an encouraging start. Our priority now is to sustain this demand across the season. This year, we have planned 13 luxury journeys throughout the season. Seven under Pride of Karnataka, three under Glimpses of Karnataka, and three under Jewels of Karnataka,” said V. Ram Prasath Manohar, Secretary, Tourism Department.
The train, launched in 2008 and discontinued in 2018, was relaunched by the incumbent regime in 2024. The 2024 and 2025 seasons saw slim demand.

The first trip under the Pride of Karnataka itinerary will start on Saturday from Krantivira Sangolli Rayanna (KSR) Railway Station and will head to Mysuru. Guests will travel to Bandipur Wildlife Sanctuary, Mysuru Palace, Halebeedu, Chikkamagalur, Hampi, Goa, and finally back to Bengaluru on day 6.
Rooms for guests have been redesigned. They now comprise a living room and a bedroom, unlike previous versions where there were only bedrooms.

The food menu on the train has been diversified and made multi-cuisine based on feedback from earlier guests. Jain and gluten-free options will also be available at two onboard restaurants, Ruchi and Nalapaka, apart from alcohol at the onboard bar, Madira. “We have also modernised the onboard kitchen with a combi oven, high-capacity induction systems, and an upgraded RO water purification plant,” a senior KSTDC official said.

“This year, we have upgraded the services by training our staff in skills that are required to treat guests coming from different States and countries. Individual cabins have been provided to service providers. There will be more than 60 members in the service team working on the train,” the official said.

“Our objective is to offer world-class hospitality while showcasing the diversity of Karnataka through a carefully curated journey and position the Golden Chariot strongly in domestic and international premium tourism markets,” said Karnataka Tourism Minister K. J. George.

articles.title: Two Maharashtra Ekikaran Samiti leaders arrested in Belagavi
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Police arrested two Maharashtra Ekikaran Samiti (MES) youth wing leaders Shubham Shelke and Manohar Hundri charging them with offences under provisions of the Prevention of Atrocities against SC/ST Act, in Belagavi on October 22.

Officers from the Khadebazar police station took them into custody in connection with a case filed in January 2025. They were produced in court that remanded them to judicial custody till November 4. They were taken to the Hindalga Central prison.

Raju Talwar, a leader of the Walmiki yuvaka Sangha, had registered the complaint, alleging that two had used abusive language against certain SC/ST communities during a MES rally in January 2025. “They were arrested after failing to appear before the police, despite receiving notices to do so,” police said.

Mr. Shelke condemned the act, claiming the police took them into custody without issuing any prior notice. He told reporters before going to jail that this was to prevent the ‘Black Day’ observance that the MES plans on November 1, the day of Karnataka Rajyotsava. He complained that the arrest was politically motivated. He alleged that MES leaders were being harassed as they were fighting for the rights of the Marathi-speaking community.

articles.title: EU ‘inviting disaster’ by imposing carbon tax on steel, says Piyush Goyal in Berlin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The European Union (EU) is “inviting disaster” by imposing a carbon tax on its steel products , Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said in Berlin on Thursday (October 23, 2026).

Participating in the Berlin Global Dialogue, he also said the EU is “shooting” itself in the foot by bringing in more regulations, restrictions on itself, and closing its borders, something that actually helped them become a developed set of nations.
"You put a CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) on yourself. You put a 50% import duty to bring steel into your country. You're inviting disaster. Your cost of living will go up," he said.

He added that through this battery of regulations, the EU is trying to impose an artificial situation on itself, trying to create boundaries within Europe, trying to bring in "absolutely ridiculous" at times standards or levels of protection to safeguard certain sectors, steel being one of them, and only hurting its own economy.

"Now, imagine going forward, every infrastructure, whether it's a port or an airport or your autobahns in Germany or your expressways, your utilities, your water pipelines, you name the infrastructure with costlier steel, costlier aluminium, costlier cement, with all the overlay of CBAM and deforestation rules," he said.

"We've lost count. You keep adding to your regulations, add to the burden of your industry, make yourself uncompetitive. And of course, in some sense, it'll also create non-tariff barriers for others to trade with you," Mr. Goyal said.

"And I don't say that. Much bigger leaders are saying that. And in this reciprocal world, you bring in a regulation and stop some other country from working with you. They'll bring in two regulations, which will hurt your businesses," he said.
He added that at the end of the day, cost of living in Europe will go up, business competitiveness will go down and inflation will be high.

"You will not be able to compete in global markets. Your auto industry is suffering that already. I think auto sales are down from Germany by 15 or 20% in the last decade or so," the Minister said, adding, "How will you be competitive in the future? You will ultimately outprice your industry."
He added that India is working on increasing competitiveness and is also working at a win-win partnership with everybody.

"We've got fair, equitable, and balanced agreements with every one of the partners with whom we are working. At least in the last four or five years, post-2014 particularly, we're forging friendships, basis competitiveness. We are building complementary strengths," he said.
He added that India would trade with countries such as Singapore, where there is no CBAM and deforestation.

articles.title: Economics beyond the individual
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford’s work modelling the macroeconomy based on individual agents’ decisions has significant implications for monetary policy. Despite being hailed as providing a rigorous foundation for stabilisation policies, focusing on the individual blinds us to the way the macroeconomy actually works. It may seem paradoxical; John Maynard Keynes’s insight was that the aggregate economy cannot be understood simply as the sum of individual actions. Heterodox economics, by focusing on the structure of the broader economy rather than its individual components, provides a much better framework for understanding the economy.
The work of Keynes in the wake of the Great Depression led to the development of the study of the aggregate economy, as opposed to studying demand and supply of individual commodities.
Microeconomics focuses on the optimising behaviour of the individual, while macroeconomics focuses on statistical relationships to characterise aggregate behaviour.

Hall and Woodford provided rigorous models that rooted the study of macroeconomic aggregates, such as consumption, investment and employment, in the behaviour of individual agents. A key contribution was linking consumption to interest rates and the future. Individuals chose to smooth consumption over their lifetimes rather than base it solely on their current needs.

When interest rates were high, savings yielded greater returns. Individuals therefore had an incentive to defer some consumption to earn more and consume more in the future. Higher interest rates could reduce current consumption and hence lower current demand, and vice versa. Macroeconomic dynamics could consequently be derived from rigorous formulations of how individuals responded to market signals and policy variables such as interest rates.

This provided a framework within which Central Bankers could target an interest rate that was ‘neutral’ to the real economy — one that neither excessively stimulated nor depressed aggregate demand — greatly aiding the development of sophisticated stabilisation paradigms for monetary policy.

However, this approach collapsed the distinction between consumption, savings and investment. By viewing consumption inter-temporally, and by making it the main component of demand, the microfoundations methodology relegated the importance of volatile investment expectations to the background. Whatever was not consumed currently was saved, and automatically translated into future consumption demand. This was the framework followed by classical economics, which Keynes contested. He cautioned that not all saving is necessarily undertaken for future consumption.

In contrast, investment is fuelled by expectations of business owners as to prospects of profit. There is no necessity for the savings behaviour of individuals to always imply a demand for future consumption, and hence investment, by businesses. How can businesses determine whether an act of individual savings is to spend on a house for the future, or to ward against a future health emergency that may or may not occur? In such a situation, the interest rate cannot serve as an indicator of the extent of future consumption.
Keynes further suggested a radical intervention. It was not the interest rate that equated savings and investment, but income. Investment raised income, and generated an equal amount of savings.

This is not merely a technical insight, but an important way in which to view policy. It is not savings or inter-temporal consumption demand that affects output growth and employment, but business investment. To understand why economies are prone to instability, one must examine the investment behaviour of companies rather than the consumption demands of individuals.

According to Keynes, investment being done for profit in an environment of uncertainty is the chief source of economic instability. In uncertain situations, it is rational for investors to follow the herd, investing during a boom for fear of missing out on speculative returns, and withdrawing investment in a recession for fear of loss. This is the reason why booms and recessions get amplified. The work of Keynesians such as Hyman Minsky and Jan Kregel offers great insight into how the financial behaviour of firms brought about the boom in housing construction and finance, as well as the recession in 2008. Much of the current stock market gains in the U.S. economy are being driven by AI hyperscalers, giving rise to concerns of a new bubble that might eventually burst. Such outcomes can be clearly discerned when viewed from a Keynesian lens.

Some might argue that it does not matter how one views the economy, if the framework designed to bring about stability is effective. Moreover, in centering the actions of individuals, so the argument goes, this framework takes into account the reality of a complex economy being driven by individual choices.

articles.title: Why managing fiscal is a tightrope for State governments
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Kerala and Tamil Nadu are among the most socially and economically advanced States in India. Yet, the finances of both governments, like those of most other States, are under stress. The White Papers recently released by the two governments described their outstanding debt as alarming. State government debt is often vilified as the result of fiscal mismanagement. But it may, in fact, reflect a mismatch between development aspirations and the limited fiscal capacity of State governments.

Debts build up over the years with deficits, which arise when the government’s expenditure overshoots its tax and other receipts. In India, while the power to raise taxes rests largely with the Union government, a larger share of overall government spending is borne by the State governments. A majority of the State government expenditure is on social sectors, such as health and education, and economic sectors, such as agriculture and irrigation, all of which have a direct impact on people’s lives and livelihoods. In Kerala, the high levels of State government spending on social sectors since the 1960s have been a central constituent of the public action driving social progress. Compared with the corresponding average for all Indian States, per capita State government social expenditure was higher in Kerala and Tamil Nadu (by 30% and 20%, respectively). In contrast, it was markedly lower in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh (by 35% and 40%) (for the period 2020-23, according to an analysis based on State Finances: A Study of Budgets, Reserve Bank of India).

articles.title: The reality behind falling net FDI
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: I ndia’s net foreign direct investment (FDI) has declined drastically in recent years. Critics see the weak net flows as a sign of weakness, while the Chief Economic Adviser points to the large inflows and rising manufacturing FDI as evidence of strength. He links weak net flows to profit repatriation and outward investment by Indian companies.

However, this debate overlooks a major issue. By focusing on overall numbers, both sides ignore the changing composition of international capital and the Balance of Payments (BoP) mechanisms that govern inflows and outflows.

For BoP purposes, net FDI is calculated as the difference between inflows and outflows after adjusting for the repatriation of capital. From the peak of $44.0 billion in 2020-21, net FDI fell to less than $1 billion in 2024-25. It recovered to $7.6 billion in 2025-26. The corresponding gross inflow was $94.6 billion.

It is necessary to note that India’s liberal FDI policy, introduced in 1991, initially emphasised technology acquisition, export promotion, and foreign exchange conservation. Over time, policy increasingly prioritised attracting larger inflows, while concerns regarding future external payment obligations and investment quality receded.

FDI is often viewed as a uniform, long-term commitment that brings technology and management skills to the host country. FDI can fall into three different investor classes, each with distinct capabilities, strategies, and exit timelines.

The first category is real FDI (RFDI), consisting of traditional multinational enterprises with the technology, brands, and capabilities to establish production and services. These generally represent long-term commitments.

The second category comprises financial investors, including private equity funds, venture capital firms, sovereign wealth funds, and asset managers. Their main goal is capital growth and planned exits.

The third category includes diaspora investments and special purpose vehicles (SPVs). These involve capital raised abroad and funneled through offshore financial centres, sometimes including the round-tripping of Indian funds.

Data on remittance-level FDI from the past four years, from 2022-23 to 2025-26 up to December, show that RFDI made up 41.9% of “effective inflows.” Financial investors followed closely with a 40.5% share, while the remaining 17.6% came from the diaspora and SPVs linked to India.

The business model of financial investors suggests future exits that result in large-scale capital repatriations. A notable example occurred in 2025 when Singapore’s Temasek exited Schneider Electric India Ltd., earning $6.4 billion on an investment of $637 million made in 2020. Total recorded divestment in CY 2025 was $52 billion, with 45 major foreign private equity and venture capital exits accounting for $29 billion in outflows.

Based on an analysis of effective inflows, FDI in India’s manufacturing sector has declined across three consecutive four-year periods. Most notably, RFDI into manufacturing accounted for only 10.6% of total effective inflows during the most recent four-year period.

A major blind spot in gross FDI figures is the mixing of new capital injections with corporate accounting changes, such as intra-group ownership reorganisations, mergers, share swaps, and the conversion of earlier non-equity instruments such as external commercial borrowings (ECBs) and convertible debentures.

articles.title: SBI’s cyber defences: What the bank had in place
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The suspected customer-data exposure at State Bank of India (SBI) has brought its cybersecurity preparedness into focus, despite the bank reporting an extensive array of safeguards in its annual disclosures.

SBI’s FY2025–26 Sustainability Report and Annual Report, published before the reported exposure, detail its security audits, automated threat monitoring, incident-response procedures and employee training. The disclosures also outline plans to further integrate its cyber-defence operations.

SBI’s Sustainability Report says information-systems audits covered 427 IT systems during FY26. Audits of outsourced IT activities covered 695 activities, while internal and external cybersecurity audits covered 176 IT applications and infrastructure and 151 systems, respectively.
However, the report does not disclose the findings, the number of vulnerabilities identified or how many were rectified. SBI reported “nil” instances of data breaches during FY26.

The bank’s Global Cyber Security Operations Centre (GCSOC) continuously monitors critical information systems for threats and unauthorised access. Automated tracking of indicators of compromise (IoCs)—digital clues that may signal cyberattacks—has replaced a previously manual process.
SBI also monitors phishing, fraudulent websites, brand impersonation, vishing and rogue mobile applications, pursuing the removal of malicious links and websites.

Its Annual Report cites an automated Secure Configuration Monitoring System covering more than 85,000 IT assets. AI-driven intelligence platforms, risk profiling and continuous monitoring of digital transactions help identify suspicious activity.

Security testing includes ethical hacking, vulnerability assessments, penetration testing and red-team exercises across websites, mobile applications, databases, networks and internal systems. Monthly domain-password-spray tests seek to identify employees using easily guessed passwords.
Firewalls, encryption, multi-factor authentication and data-loss prevention tools provide additional safeguards.

CERT SBI serves as the central first responder to cyber incidents. Its response framework covers detection, containment, eradication, recovery and post-incident reviews. A separate Incident Response Wing handles forensic investigations, threat hunting, mock drills and regulatory reporting.

SBI conducted 2,079 information-security and cybersecurity training programmes, benefiting 39,961 employees in FY26. Nearly 1.81 lakh employees had completed mandatory cybersecurity e-learning and assessments by March 31, 2026.
Oversight rests with the Board-level IT Strategy Committee, while the Group Chief Information Security Officer heads the Information Security Department.

articles.title: Cambridge Analytica, Facebook’s ‘friend sharing’ feature, and $25 billion penalty | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The Story So Far: Meta was ordered on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) to pay a fine of $25 billion to the U.S. state of New Mexico after a jury found last month that the company had misled its users regarding data privacy, in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. This is one of the largest financial penalties imposed on a corporation in U.S. history, as well as a landmark victory holding Facebook liable under the State’s consumer protection law.

“For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez. He had sued Meta in 2021, alleging that the company misled Facebook users on who had access to their data, how the ⁠company handled hate speech and misinformation posted on its platform as well as other internal policies.

Initially, Facebook allowed third-party app developers to access personal information related to the users of these apps as well as their friends, even if they were unaware of their data being shared, through a feature called “friend sharing”. The platform publicly announced that it would end this feature in 2014 and after a transition period ending May 2015, they said that users could choose whether to share their information with the application.

However, in spite of these assurances, the platform had put in place exemptions for its “favoured partners” who would still be able to access this information, albeit without the knowledge of the users.

The now-defunct Cambridge Analytica was a British data analytics firm best known for assisting the 2016 Presidential campaign of Donald Trump. The firm acquired data on millions of Facebook users via means that deceived both the users and Facebook, according to media reports. This data was reportedly used to undertake targeted political advertising.

The data was harvested using a third-party personality quiz app called “thisisyourdigitallife,” which was installed by about 2,70,000 users, but also collected information on their friends. The app reached roughly 87 million Facebook users globally.

Although Facebook learned in December 2015 that Cambridge Analytica had obtained the data, it was not publicly disclosed until 2018, after a whistleblower came forward, triggering a major political scandal.

Following the revelations, Facebook assured that it would conduct an “App Developer Investigation” (ADI). Among the assurances given as part of ADI was an inquiry into all apps that had access to user data prior to the 2014 platform change and ensuring the deletion of improperly obtained data. However, it was later revealed that the platform did not conduct the comprehensive probe that it had promised. Moreover, it did not have the ability to conduct such a thorough investigation or enforce deletion of data.

Facebook had also committed to notifying users about data breach. Its investigation found at least 2,000 unique apps associated with data misuse. Out of this, it was able to associate 1,585 applications with New Mexico user accounts. Those affected the data of at least 11,46,225 New Mexican Facebook users. However, it was found that Facebook did not inform the user about this.

The New Mexico jury found in September 2026 that Facebook violated the State’s Unfair Practices Act 43,899,725 times. The 26 representations that the jury found violative and wilful span a period of 11 years — May 24, 2010 to August 18, 2021. Among these representations were those made by Facebook’s senior leadership including Mark Zuckerberg, CEO, and Sheryl Sandberg, the then-COO.

Taking these factors into consideration, the New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties. The judge said that a penalty of more than $219 billion would be justified under state ⁠law, which allows a $5,000 penalty for each violation, but he reduced the amount. He also ordered that the penalty shall accrue an annual interest of 15% until it was paid in full. Meta said penalties of no more than $3.45 billion were warranted.
The Court further said that it will “reserve on injunctive relief pending further briefing in this matter”.

articles.title: EU ‘inviting disaster’ by imposing carbon tax on steel, says Piyush Goyal in Berlin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The European Union (EU) is “inviting disaster” by imposing a carbon tax on its steel products , Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said in Berlin on Thursday (October 23, 2026).

Participating in the Berlin Global Dialogue, he also said the EU is “shooting” itself in the foot by bringing in more regulations, restrictions on itself, and closing its borders, something that actually helped them become a developed set of nations.
"You put a CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism) on yourself. You put a 50% import duty to bring steel into your country. You're inviting disaster. Your cost of living will go up," he said.

He added that through this battery of regulations, the EU is trying to impose an artificial situation on itself, trying to create boundaries within Europe, trying to bring in "absolutely ridiculous" at times standards or levels of protection to safeguard certain sectors, steel being one of them, and only hurting its own economy.

"Now, imagine going forward, every infrastructure, whether it's a port or an airport or your autobahns in Germany or your expressways, your utilities, your water pipelines, you name the infrastructure with costlier steel, costlier aluminium, costlier cement, with all the overlay of CBAM and deforestation rules," he said.

"We've lost count. You keep adding to your regulations, add to the burden of your industry, make yourself uncompetitive. And of course, in some sense, it'll also create non-tariff barriers for others to trade with you," Mr. Goyal said.

"And I don't say that. Much bigger leaders are saying that. And in this reciprocal world, you bring in a regulation and stop some other country from working with you. They'll bring in two regulations, which will hurt your businesses," he said.
He added that at the end of the day, cost of living in Europe will go up, business competitiveness will go down and inflation will be high.

"You will not be able to compete in global markets. Your auto industry is suffering that already. I think auto sales are down from Germany by 15 or 20% in the last decade or so," the Minister said, adding, "How will you be competitive in the future? You will ultimately outprice your industry."
He added that India is working on increasing competitiveness and is also working at a win-win partnership with everybody.

"We've got fair, equitable, and balanced agreements with every one of the partners with whom we are working. At least in the last four or five years, post-2014 particularly, we're forging friendships, basis competitiveness. We are building complementary strengths," he said.
He added that India would trade with countries such as Singapore, where there is no CBAM and deforestation.

articles.title: Women are protesting around Poland for free access to legal abortions
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Women plan street demonstrations in more than 20 Polish cities and towns on Thursday (October 22, 2026) to protest the lack of access to free and legal abortion.

They're accusing Prime Minister Donald Tusk's liberal government of failing to fulfil its promise to relax Poland's strict abortion laws, and are protesting even though the Parliament passed two bills on Tuesday (October 20) aimed at easing abortion rules. The measures are likely to be vetoed by the conservative president, Karol Nawrocki.

Passing the draft laws now, a year before the next parliamentary election, is a case of “token gestures” rather than a genuine effort to reform abortion law, said Zofia Marcinek of the Abortion Dream Team, a reproductive rights activist group in Warsaw.

She said the liberal government knew the draft laws stood no chance of withstanding Nawrocki's veto, and has merely tried to create the impression of taking action because it needs women's support to win elections next year.
Since 1993, legal abortions have been allowed in Catholic Poland only in cases of severe fetal abnormality, risk to the mother's life and health, or the pregnancy being a result of rape or incest.
Polish women have been pushing for the legalisation of abortion ever since, including in a nationwide wave of demonstrations of women wearing black called “Black Protest,” which began in 2016.

Rather than being liberalised, Poland's abortion laws were tightened further, banning abortions of fetuses with congenital defects in 2020 under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.

Despite the laws, abortions remain common in Poland, an overwhelming majority of which are carried out by women at home using pills obtained from outside the country. Women who undergo abortions, including by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility under Polish law. But people helping them, including doctors and family, can potentially be prosecuted.
And abortion remains a taboo subject in Poland, which now has one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws, with only Malta imposing stricter limits.

PM Tusk's pro-European coalition won the 2023 election in part on a promise to liberalise Poland's abortion laws. But in 2024, Mr. Tusk said his government wouldn't be able to overcome the likely veto of a conservative president. Instead, measures were introduced to prevent hospitals from refusing to perform legal abortions on religious grounds.
"The state will increasingly effectively stand on the side of the woman when she is making dramatic decisions in her life,” Mr. Tusk said in 2024 when he announced the measures.

Polish hospitals performed 573 abortions in the first half of 2026, compared to 452 in all of 2022, before Mr. Tusk came to power, according to data from the National Health Fund. But activists say tens of thousands of abortions happen yearly outside of hospitals.

articles.title: Elon Musk's political baggage clouds prospects for SpaceX-Tesla deal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: A possible merger between Elon Musk’s rocket ​company SpaceX and carmaker Tesla may face bigger obstacles from politics than from regulation, drawing scrutiny in Beijing and potentially igniting a battle between US President Donald Trump ‌and the Democrats.

Musk revived speculation about a tie-up this week, calling a combination “a good idea” and confirming that ​committees at both companies were reviewing a potential deal, a step toward what could become the largest merger in history ⁠and create a company worth about $3.5 trillion.

But a merger would also unite one of the US government’s most important aerospace and defense contractors with one of the most China-exposed major American manufacturers — a combination likely to raise questions about national security risks both in Washington and in Beijing.
Those concerns are unlikely to derail a deal, ‌analysts said, but they would likely leave the combined company exposed to years of political wrangling and pressure from both sides of the Pacific.

Tesla’s China operations, they said, could become a source of leverage for Beijing in any future dispute with ‌Washington, while a Democratic takeover of the US House of Representatives in next month’s midterm elections could subject the deal to congressional investigations and ‌political ⁠maneuvering.
Democrats immediately raised concerns about the deal’s implications, signaling their intent to turn the merger into a political flashpoint ahead ⁠of the November 3 midterms.

“If Elon Musk moves forward with the merger of Tesla and SpaceX, the deal would carry real risks that antitrust enforcers across the world would scrutinize,” said US Senator Cory Booker, a New Jersey Democrat who sits on both the Judiciary and Foreign Relations committees.

He added that he was prepared to conduct oversight of ​any deal: “When one person controls the infrastructure that governments and militaries ‌depend on, his business decisions become national security decisions, too.”
Musk could seek to address concerns by limiting how closely the two companies are integrated.

The greater threat to the deal may come later, however, if a future administration takes a harder line on the relationship between Tesla and a company increasingly tied to US national security, analysts said.
“A merger agreement would involve pledges of limits to the connections between SpaceX ‌and Tesla,” said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

“I don’t think the Trump administration would enforce ​these limits. However, the next administration could certainly begin to scrutinize a merged entity. This may be the biggest risk to a deal - that it could get unwound in 2029.”

articles.title: Celebrating forgotten women who helped improved maternal health
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The debate in the scientific world has often been about glory. Who deserves the glory for a discovery, for an invention, for defining a procedure, a drug, a vaccine? Does credit ever attach to the patients who were experimented upon, the participants of a clinical trial, people who gave of their time and body in order that science may advance, in order that people who come after them do not suffer. Codes of ethics are mutable, they keep changing, and the grant of credit in science also operates on this arc. This story is a page from such an omission, a blunder. Nearly 150 years later, some form of reparation was attempted.

For the world, for the longest time, perhaps even till today, J. Marion Sims was the ‘Father of Modern Gynaecology.’ Sims reportedly earned the title for his ‘groundbreaking surgical innovations, notably the development of a cure for vesicovaginal fistula.” For his achievements, Sims not only received the soubriquet, but also statues and memorials and hospitals and wards named after him. The number of girls on whom he perfected his techniques were not even a footnote in the glorious history he covered himself with.

Among them was Anarcha Westcott, a teenage mother, a patient who developed a terrible vesicovaginal fistula, tears or holes that develop between the bladder and vagina, sustained after three days of labour. The tears made it impossible to control her bowel or bladder and the condition caused her immense pain and suffering. That is how she came under the ‘care’ of Sims, if care could be used to describe what he went on to do.

Anarcha was a young African American woman wrested down in slavery. Sims reportedly believed that African American women do not feel pain, so he experimented on her repeatedly (we know of two others -- Betsey, and Lucy), operating without anaesthesia (though it was available). Sims himself records that he had performed nearly 30 procedures on her, consent was a casualty of the times, before he perfected his technique using silver to suture the fistula, that prevented infection.Before this, a vesicovaginal fistula was considered untreatable, and women would continue to suffer the rest of their life.

Anarcha did not disappear after this though. J. C. Hallman, in his 2023 book S ay Anarcha- A Young Woman, a Devious Surgeon, and the Harrowing Birth of Modern Women’s Health, d id extensive research to uncover that far from disappearing after the Sims experiments, she went on to serve in Sims hospital, as a midwife, nurse, and ‘doctor woman’ to her own people, women who were also slaves. Many decades after Anarcha died, a groundswell of support arose for her from women who objected to the way she was quietly erased from history, and instead calling for her to be celebrated as the “mother of gynaecology.”

S ay Anarcha excavates history, deconstructing the biographical smoke screen of a surgeon who has falsely been enshrined as a medical pioneer and bringing forth a heroic Black woman to her rightful place at the center of the creation story of modern women’s health care. She was more than a medical ‘specimen’, she worked at Sims’ slave hospital near Montgomery, Alabama. She trained and served as a surgical nurse and went on to help other women, also being experimented upon at the hospital.

More recently, efforts have been made to honour her contribution to gynaecology. The American college of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists have dedicated two days – February 28 and March 1—to Anarcha, Lucy and Betsey. Recognition also saw expression in art: At Harvard’s Hutchins Center exhibition in 2023, a prominent exhibit was artist Jules Arthur’s paintings of Anarcha, Luch and Betsey through her work titled “Call and Response: A Narrative of Reverence to Our Foremothers in Gynaecology“.

Artist Michelle Browder created a 15-foot public monument honouring them as “the mothers of gynaecology“ in downtown Montgomery. Tangentially, it was also seen as a victory that Sims’ statue was removed from Central Park in April 2018 and relocated. Hallman’s book was preceded by a documentary Remembering Anarcha.

Unfortunately, Anarcha’s story is not merely a historical wrong. It serves to remind health practitioners and policy makers that several inequities still govern access and affordability of high quality care; that for women, it could be tougher than it might be for men. For that, we will have to keep saying her name, so it will be a reminder. Say her name, say Anarcha.

articles.title: Microsoft develops AI tool that can diagnose 'sequentially' like a doctor
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Microsoft researchers say an AI tool that diagnoses patients step by step, as doctors do, was more than ​twice as accurate as general physicians at solving complex medical cases, according ‌to a study published on Thursday in Science.

The model ​identifies and coordinates the questions that should be asked ⁠of a patient, as well as the exams and tests that should be ordered, using an “orchestrator” that organises how AI will tackle a problem by ‌employing a simulated panel of clinical experts collaborating to solve diagnostic cases, according to the report.
Existing medical AI models typically ‌take an all-at-once approach that examines all of a patient’s ‌symptoms, ⁠lab results and imaging studies to generate a diagnosis.

With ⁠the orchestrator coordinating the steps to reaching a diagnosis, the AI model first decides what to ask about the patient’s history and what is significant in the ​physical exam. Based on what it ‌learns, it decides which tests to order, considers the results, and orders further testing as appropriate.
All the while, it is updating its working hypotheses and plans, the research leaders said in an ‌interview.

Tasked with diagnosing more than 300 highly unusual and confusing ​medical dilemmas, the model employing the diagnostic orchestrator was more than twice as accurate at “working up” the patient and ⁠determining the diagnosis as general physicians using textbooks and the internet.
The tool also outperformed human physicians when presented with scenarios drawn from a ‌major database of emergency room admissions.
Assessments comparing these types of older systems to human doctors usually use multiple-choice questions, the researchers said.
“AI has become very good at getting a 100% pass rate on those,” said Dr. Dominic King, the corporate vice president of the health unit at Microsoft AI, whose team is developing the new technology.
“But ‌of course, that’s not real-world. No patient ever came to see me with ​a nice summary.”
The researchers also found that diagnostic processes cost less when the orchestrator designs the work-ups than ⁠when human doctors do.
“We’re not just measuring the accuracy of the systems. ⁠We’re also measuring how judiciously and carefully it goes through a diagnostic work-up,” said Harsha Nori, head of AI at ‌Microsoft AI Health.

articles.title: An Indian woman phytochemist without parallel
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Did you know that an Indian woman scientist had a notable role to play in the development of anti-epileptic drugs and anti-malarial drugs? That the same woman also told us most of what we needed to know about the medicinal plants in the subcontinent?

By the standards of her time, unlike other women scientists, Asima Chatterjee did get recognition for her research while she was alive, but it cannot be said that she received the adulation and celebration that her male peers did. That doesn’t make Asima Chatterjee any less tall a figure in the history of Indian science, and the nation must be grateful for her pioneering work in organic chemistry and the sub category of phytomedicine – using plant extracts to treat various conditions, even prevent them.

109 years ago, Asima Chatterjee was born, on September 23. Her love affair with chemistry began at a young age and she went on to pursue this, with a Bacherlor’s degree and a masters in the subject. At a time when few women were able to take up higher education, she went on to complete her Doctor of Science degree in pre-independent India, specialising in phytochemistry. History records her as the first Indian woman to be awarded a Doctor of Science by any Indian university. She went on to gain expertise in research methodology at the University of Wisconsin, Madison and the California Institute of Technology, working with international experts in the field before returning to India.

She took a great interest in a sector that sought to harness the natural plant biodiversty of India and phytochemistry skills to develop newer compounds and drugs that could be used to treat people. Today plant-based extracts form key elements of critical drugs. Plant-derived drugs range from pure compounds extracted from herbs to complex botanical extracts approved as prescription medications. Chatterjee sank herself into the development of clinically useful drugs from indigenous plants – striking success with isolating the chemical constituents of Marsdenia tinctoria – which led to the formulation of the anti-epileptic drug later marketed as Ayush- 56.

Chatterjee also made huge breakthroughs in developing anti-malarial drugs derived from plant extracts. But the greatest achievement that she is credited with is her extensive research on the chemistry of alkaloids found in Caranthus roseus, or the Madagascar periwinkle, which contributed leaps to the understanding of compounds with anti-cancer properties. No less important is the foundation she laid for modern pharmaceutical chemistry, utilising physical and chemical methods to to determine the complex molecular structures of numerous organic compounds, and recording her methodology meticulously.

Beyond her pioneering work in the lab, Chatterjee was also an ace institution builder and educationist. During her academic career, she served as a professor of chemistry at the University of Calcutta at a time of intense gender barriers in academia, and was later appointed as the Khaira Professor of Chemistry, a prestigious chair in the varsity.

Her work in science was recognised with a Padma Bhushan in 1975, Chatterjee creating a record here too, being the first woman scientist to achieve this honour. She was the first female scientist to be elected as the General President of the Indian Science Congress Association and was also a Fellow of the Indian National Science Academy. No wonder then that she was the first female recipient of the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in Chemical Sciences (1961), India’s top science award, introduced in 1958. She was also awarded the prestigious CV Raman Award and PC Ray Award.

Today, as the debate rages about bringing scientific vigour and scientifically validating traditional systems of medicine in the country, Chatterjee was a beacon even in this area, her work bridged the gap between traditional Ayurvedic knowledge and modern rigorous chemical analysis, to benefit humanity. Legacy

But Asima Chatterjee’s achievements cannot be confined to just the scientific arena, her immense achievement must also be counted at a time when formidable gender barriers stood in the way of female achievements, breaking the glass ceiling and making it possible, even inspiring, generations of women scientists to make their bold foray into the sciences. Being that rare Indian women scientist who got substantial recognition during their lifetime, in the scientific world, and yet she was largely missing from mainstream narratives, and global histories of science.

But today, we say her name, properly celebrate her legacy. Asima Chatterjee, exceptional chemist, phytochemist and extraordinary pioneering scientist who opened the portals the world of science for generations of women. Say her name, say Asima Chatterjee.

articles.title: India’s first woman Surgeon General fought for a place in science
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Early 1900s India was a place where your gender determined what you could be in life. That nation could not stomach the thought of, trivial as it was, common as it is today, a woman pursuing the sciences. This antediluvian thought though, this kind of restriction was only the cause of a temporary disruption Mary Poonen Lukose’s path to glory.

It is inescapable irony that India’s first woman Surgeon General Mary Poonen Lukose was not allowed to study science. Born in Ayamanam (incidentally, Arundathi Roy’s backdrop in the God of Small Things ) in Kottayam in 1886, Mary was so bright, she topped the matriculation exam. Nevermind how bright she was, her gender was a disqualifier as Maharaja College in Tiruvananthapuram declined her admission to the sciences. Only a temporary detour, Mary went on to get a degree in history, becoming the first woman from Travancore to graduate from Madras University in 1909.

However, her family could afford to send her to London to pursue medicine, and she was the first Indian woman to graduate in Medicine from the University of London, according to an article published by Cambridge University Press (CUP) as part of a compendium of Modern Asian Studies. She earned an MBBS from the University of London in 1915, trained in obstetrics and gynaecology, and studied paediatrics at Great Ormond Street Hospital.

Reports of her life, rendered through an autobiographical account, T railblazer, r eleased in 2020, record Mary as working hard in Dublin at the Rotunda Hospital, coping with the increasing work load created by the outbreak of World War 1 in 1914. When her mentor and guide, her father passed away in 1916, Mary was shattered; she had to take a call on whether she would continue in England or come back home to serve her people. She, of course, decided to come home and blazed a path of glory, only long forgotten. She returned to Travancore in 1916 as its first woman doctor.

The CUP article further quotes from an autobiographical note penned by Mary herself: “In her autobiographical essay, Mary Poonen Lukose reflects on her decision to become a doctor. She traces it to her early experiences helping out in hospitals where her father worked as a doctor, and to his example and influence on her. ‘As I grew up, he made it a point to instill into me the spirit of service to humanity.’

The article further notes that the style of her 1916 job application, her requests for references, and the correspondence surrounding it suggest that she was aware of the fact that her qualifications were exceptional for an Indian woman of her time.

Mary Poonen Lukose went on to build the scaffolding of modern public health in Travancore, one that can be attributed to the many advances that Kerala has achieved today in health care indicators. Her work helped lay the ground for what we now celebrate as the “Kerala model” of health—fronting strong primary care, institutional childbirth, public health outreach, and unusually good social indicators. Acknowledging her contributions, in the 2018 budget speech, the finance minister of the State said, on record, in the House: ‘Dr. Mary Poonen Lukose is one of the most talented people in the development of Kerala’s health system.’

At the Women and Children Hospital in Thycaud, Mary worked as an obstetrician and superintendent, initiating daughters of local birth attendants into training midwifery, an attempt to subsume traditional midwifery into scientific deliveries and maternal care. Some historic references to her indicate she performed Travancore’s first Caesarean section before 1920, reportedly sometimes working only by the light of a hurricane-lamp light.

As Surgeon General from 1938, she was responsible for 32 government hospitals, 40 dispensaries, and 20 private institutions. In colonial era India, this could be notched up as a mega achievement for a woman, not only in health care, but also an administrator. Mary also founded a tuberculosis sanatorium in Nagercoil, and established the X-Ray and Radium Institute in Tiruvananthapuram.

It was not only for the issue of providing women adequate health facilities that she lent her voice, but was equally vociferous on women’s political rights. She herself, in 1922, was nominated to Travancore’s legislative council, becoming the State’s first woman legislator.

But Mary was a multi-splendored person, capable of achievements across sectors. As the nuns sing in the Sound of Music of Maria the reluctant nun: How do you catch a cloud and pin it down? Mary co-founded the Tiruvananthapuram branch of the Young Women’s Christian Association and served as its president for 50 years. She was also a member of two professional bodies, the Indian Medical Association and the Federation of Obstetric and Gynaecological Societies of India.
Many honours came her way, including the Vaidyaśāstrakuśala by the Maharaja of Travancore in 1935, and the Padma Śhri in 1975, just a year before her death at the age of 90.

articles.title: HeLa to a new world where progress in science matches dignity for patient
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: They also serve science, who are not scientists. One of science’s most egregious instances of epistemic dominance, where a powerful institution overrode and exploited a marginalised individual - was Henrietta Lacks – donor of the famous, immortal HeLa cell line . Cells extracted from her, without permission, transformed medical research, but her story was ignored, erased and obscured for decades. The scientific world that generously used this unique cell line for successful research into virology, vaccines, genetics and even cancer care, but the erasure of the donor of those cells was historic in its completeness.

Lacks, an African American tobacco farmer from southern United States, sought treatment at the ‘coloured ward’ in Johns Hopkins Centre for cervical cancer, way back in 1951. While it was common for medical professionals, in those days, to take samples and cells without the express permission of the patient, particularly if it was an African American woman, these cells were different. Johns Hopkins used the cells from her tumour to culture a line of cells that was extraordinarily durable outside the body. Usually human cells die outside of the body. Anonymised by a laboratory acronymn, Lacks’ cells (HeLa) turned out to be the first human cells to successfully grow, divide, and survive indefinitely outside the human body.

HeLa was a miracle that scientists had chanced upon. With HeLa, they could mass produce human cells in a standard format that could be used for biomedical research, and would underpin several breakthrough discoveries, that would revolutionise medical care. No one knew, however, of the immense exploitation behind this miracle cell line, and the profound lack of consent in procuring the samples.

Lacks, who died at merely 31 years, and was buried in an unmarked grave, remained invisible, not even a footnote, completely uncredited and her family entirely in the dark about her contribution to the world of science. Henrietta Lacks’ family first learned about her cells in nearly quarter of a century later, when scientists reached out to them, requesting blood samples once they suspected that the HeLa cell line had contaminated other research samples. This came as a bolt on the family, who could not fathom how cells from their mother had survived this long outside of her, and how this strange situation had come to be. While the academic world and several sections of the corporate world benefited richly from the HeLa cell line, Lacks’ own family had remained entrenched in poverty and struggling to make ends meet. The struggle of the family to come to terms with this exploitation, and the battles they had to fight with the system and science itself is well curated by Rebecca Sloot in her best selling book T he Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks.

In the 1950s, bioethical norms, particularly around informed consent were either non existent, or, at best, weak. But, in this particular case, Lacks was a black farmer from a rural unit, being treated in a segregated section in a large hospital. Consequently, an entrenched rascism, still alive in the southern United States in the 50s, and class bias contributed in good measure to the shabby treatment of this very valuable patient. Unhesitatingly and boldly, Sloot dragged this out into the open, through the book, knocking on the consciousness of the world and science, biomedical research, urging a discussion, a debate and at the end of it, a nod to what happened. It took years before these units would shamefully acknowledge the great injustice meted out to Lacks’ and her family.

The book, published in 2010, drew attention to the larger debate of patient rights and bodily autonomy. Sloot also underlined the fact that donors need to be acknowledged, heralding a new woke world of bio ethics, laboratory practices and the responsibilities of researchers. No longer could a moral failure be allowed to take patients for a ride, rules and regulations should replace the conscience and a situation like this would hopefully never happen again.

But this story does not end this way. After nearly 75 years of fighting this battle, the Lacks’ family finally found some closure. Reparation was finally achieved with the family settling with Johns Hopkins and other associated institutions in a landmark agreement that firstly acknowledged harm had been done, and also included measures to compensate the family and honour Lacks’ role in science. This included significant financial recompense, and involving the family into research using HeLa cells.

This agreement did reinforce the supremacy of informed consent practices, thus refining research ethics policy, but it also expanded the involvement of the patient and the community in research work. The Lacks’ family success is a milestone of sorts in biomedical research, with calls now being made to improve how institutions and labs credit how their biological materials, and also look at reparative action for families historically exploited by science.

Lacks’ story is a cautionary tale for science. It’s a reckoning with what has historically gone wrong, to set some wrongs right , and make sure the violations of the past are not repeated, but do inform the future, so that scientific progress can proceed without losing respect for human dignity. For this stupendous achievement, we have Henrietta Lacks to thank. From being denied even the footnote in history, she has created a brave new world in science.

articles.title: Canary in the coal mine: On the performance of India’s core industrial sectors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The latest data on the performance of the core industrial sectors show the economy may be facing an industrial uptick, but questions about its sustainability remain. Growth in the Index of Core Industries rose to a series-high of 7.9% in September 2026, the second consecutive month of accelerated performance. Any such improvement is to be celebrated, but a deeper look at what is driving it is also warranted. The coal sector saw growth suddenly shoot up to 10.7% in September. The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. The electricity sector grew 11.4% in September, capping off a half-year dominated by double-digit growth. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. The uptick in steel did, however, result in a return to double-digit growth for the iron ore sector, which should bode well for the mining component of the larger Index of Industrial Production.

The performance of the crude oil, natural gas, and refinery products sectors also highlights the fiscal problems India faces. At a time when the crude oil and natural gas sectors have both contracted continuously since 2024, refinery output rose to 10.3% in September. This means that the refineries were increasingly processing expensive imported oil. India’s oil imports in September were up 7% by volume but jumped 47% in terms of value due to the high price of oil. This is set to worsen. The attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have already pushed global oil prices above $112 a barrel, almost a six-month high. The reprieve from the U.S. on potential tariffs linked to imports of Russian oil provide India a reliable source, but the days of discounts are long gone. It is the time of premium pricing, and each barrel imported is eating into India’s foreign exchange reserves, which are also being used to defend the rupee. Cement and steel are the only sustainably growing core sectors, and those too are based on government infrastructure spending. At a time when industrial output is only temporarily propped up, the government’s fiscal space is fast shrinking.

articles.title: Tunnelling through: On China’s export control list, tunnel-boring machines
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Chinese Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs decision to place tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) on an export control list reveals a blind spot in India’s supply chain diversification. The curbs include TBMs, walking excavators, and high-altitude wet shotcrete machines. From November 18, if a shipment is intended for countries or regions deemed sensitive due to ongoing disputes with China, exporters will need an export licence from commerce authorities. For other countries/regions, exporters will need to be registered, obtain an export certificate, and submit end-use declarations stating that the equipment will not be re-routed to sensitive locations. While China has cornered around 70% of the global TBM market, prominent manufacturers in the West also maintain substantial component supply chains in the country to cut manufacturing overhead. Further, TBMs are complex to build as they have to be configured to geological characteristics at the project site and perform numerous tasks. Where a suitable TBM exists, it can be used for civilian or military purposes. India has struggled with TBM-related hold-ups with China for at least two years now, including for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project. Germany’s Herrenknecht AG set up an assembling and refurbishing facility in Chennai in 2007-08. TBM production economics differ significantly from conventional construction equipment as new plants need a minimum number of orders and must be able to access the industrial capability required to design, manufacture and repair specialised components.

However, even though India is one of the world’s largest TBM importers, expecting every sophisticated machine to be produced domestically will send public infrastructure costs soaring. Even now, depending on China’s decision on the TBMs set for India, India may have to redirect its procurement to facilities based directly in Germany or Japan, say, and absorb the higher capital cost. The BEML experience shows that manufacturing partnerships can fail without secure licensing arrangements and access to sustained demand. India should pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships, e.g., making equipment in the country under agreement with established foreign firms, and develop shared industrial capabilities rather than singular ‘national champions’, as TBM manufacturers and their suppliers can benefit from access to common testing and precision manufacturing infrastructure. Overall, Beijing is systematically identifying sectors where it commands a significant global capacity and establishing export controls to counter western technological restrictions, such as on advanced semiconductors, so any critical infrastructure sector relying on Chinese supply lines will face a compounding geopolitical risk.

articles.title: Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

articles.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.
